newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: AUSTRALIA DEPLORES PNG ARMED FORCES MOVE: HOWARD
The Prime Minister says the attempt by Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to remove the head of the country's armed forces is understandable and justifiable.
Mr Howard has told Parliament Australia utterly deplores the attempt by Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok to defy the authority of the elected Government.

But Mr Howard says the Australian High Commission in Port Moresby has reiterated to the PNG Government and the new acting commander of the PNG defence forces that Australia strongly opposes the use of mercenaries in the region.
Describing the situation in PNG as fragile, Mr Howard said the use of mercenaries would have serious consequences for the relationship between Australian and PNG.
And Foreign Minister Alexander Downer has urged Papua New Guinea to resolve the crisis peacefully and in accordance with the constitution, as soon as possible.
NEW WARNING OVER CYCLONE
People in North Queensland are being advised to complete preparations for a possible onslaught by Severe Tropical Cyclone Justin.
The Weather Bureau says the cyclone could drift west later in the week.
It's currently almost stationary about 12-hundred kilometres east-north-east of Cooktown.
The Bureau's Deputy regional director Jeff Crane says the cyclone has intensified to Category three, with very destructive winds near the centre.
He says people should not become complacent about the chance of it crossing the coast.
HOWARD STILL HOPES TO HAVE WIK RESPONSE BY EASTER
The Prime Minister has told his party colleagues he still hopes to have reached a position on the Wik decision by around Easter.
The response to the Wik decision dominated the National Party's meeting in Canberra this morning, with M-Ps reinforcing their support for existing pastoral leases to be validated.
Mr Howard hasn't ruled the National Party's position in or out.
He says the Government's position should be finalised either just before or just after Easter.
He's been having talks with relevant parties including Aboriginal groups, farmers and State Premiers and says the discussions have been going reasonably well so far.
SHORT TO RESIGN FROM PARLIAMENT
Victorian Senator Jim Short is to resign from Parliament to take up a banking post in London.

Senator Short, who was forced to resign as Assistant Treasurer late last year over his share ownership, is to be one of Australia's representatives at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Senator Short, who's been in Parliament since 1984, will take up the three year appointment in May.
NUMBER OF DELEGATES CHANGED
The Federal Government's changed the number of delegates from the States and Territories that will attend the people's convention on the republic later this year.
The Northern Territory and the ACT will have two delegates each instead of one each.
The total number of delegates will still be 76 -- half elected and half appointed by the Government.
The voting system has also been changed, and both above the line and below the line voting will be allowed, as for Senate elections.
It's been confirmed that the deposit for people wanting to stand as candidates will be 500-dollars.
The Prime Minister is expected to introduce the legislation to Parliament next Wednesday.
SMITH SAYS GOVT CAN'T RELEASE DETAILS
Former Victorian Finance Minister Ian Smith, says details of the out-of-court settlement to his former lover Cheryl Smith, can't be released unless all parties agree.
The State Opposition is expected to quiz the Government in question time today, about whether taxpayers' money was used to pay out Mr Smith's ex-lover.
Ms Harris says it's up to the Premier, Jeff Kennett, to release details of the confidential settlement.
Mr Smith says while he's happy to have the information made public, the State Government can't do it without Ms Harris' consent.
GREG NORMAN SHAKEN BY PRESIDENT'S FALL
World number one Greg Norman says it has been tough handling the fact the President of the United States had a serious fall at the golfer's Florida home.
Bill Clinton had to have surgery for a torn knee tendon after he slipped on the front steps of Norman's home at the weekend.
Norman says there was nothing he could have done to prevent the accident but he feels guilty, and is still coming to terms with emotional drain of the whole incident.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
